A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniSpatial and contain complete, readable main text and appendices A–G. Corresponding methods, experiments, equations, tables, and figures can be matched, including the rasterized appendix examples in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original model and human evaluations, PointGraph and SpatialCoT experiments, and prompting/evaluation ablations in Tables 2–5.

after.justification: V2 retains original evaluations and adds supervised-training comparisons, VSI-Bench transfer results, full-benchmark evaluations, and human agreement and uncertainty estimates.

M1.justification: Section 3.3.1 revises PointGraph's described extraction component from SAM-based segmentation to Florence-2-style object grounding. Scene-graph augmentation and InstantMesh-based SpatialCoT remain; JSON encoding and the six-view collage receive fuller explanation. Figure 5 still labels SAM, leaving the implementation used for the retained results unclear.

E1.justification: V2 adds actual evaluation on VSI-Bench, extending coverage to indoor, video-based spatial tasks including appearance order, distance and size estimation, and route planning (Table 6). Section 3.2.1 also reports incorporating SpatialViz, PhysBench, ViewSpatial, and DrivingVQA samples. OmniSpatial's four categories and 50-subtype taxonomy remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The existing model roster and CoT comparators are retained. New training experiments introduce a 200K template-corpus comparator (Table 5) and a comparison using the SpaceR-7B pipeline without added OmniSpatial supervision (Table 6). These substantially extend comparative scope to the value of training supervision.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates a 1,533-question benchmark without a training split. V2 specifies 6.9K training and 1.5K test questions, adds evaluation on all 8.4K questions, and introduces supervised-training and cross-benchmark protocols. Existing prompting and answer-scoring procedures remain; relabeling retained tables as OmniSpatial-test does not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 4.4 examines whether curated supervision teaches spatial skills through comparison with a much larger template corpus, and tests transfer using the SpaceR-7B pipeline with and without OmniSpatial. These add substantive data-quality and generalization analyses. Existing PointGraph, SpatialCoT, and prompting/evaluation ablations are retained.

E5.justification: V1 reports five-run model averages and human point estimates. V2 additionally reports Krippendorff's alpha by category and overall, and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for human accuracy (Section C.3, Table 9). These introduce annotation-reliability and uncertainty reporting; the stated five-run model practice is unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 adds training results, including 48.12 versus 40.30 for fine-tuned versus zero-shot Qwen-VL2.5-3B, and VSI-Bench scores of 43.68 versus 41.68 with versus without added OmniSpatial supervision. Table 8 adds full-dataset results under a different setting. Retained model and CoT scores are unchanged, but Table 2 revises human subtask values, including manipulation from 96.53 to 94.62, while retaining the 92.63 overall score.

T1.justification: The visual-spatial reasoning mapping and its input/output conditions in Section 2 are retained; v2 merely numbers the equation. The taxonomy receives explanatory rewriting, but neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and no substantive mathematical development is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion update the dataset contribution from approximately 1.5K to 8.4K question-answer pairs and foreground PointGraph and SpatialCoT. These methods were already contributions in v1. The four-part taxonomy, 50 subtasks, and central claim of substantial model–human performance gaps remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 newly interprets training results as evidence for curated supervision and transferable spatial skills rather than template fitting. Section C.2 adds interpretations of model-specific strengths and potential ensembling or distillation benefits, while C.3 argues for annotation consistency and a reliable human reference. Existing limitations concerning long videos and modest method improvements remain.

D1.justification: V2 specifies scene-graph encoding and query concatenation, explains the SpatialCoT input construction, and documents human evaluation procedures such as randomized options, independent responses, three annotators per item, and majority voting. Prompts and project/code/dataset links are retained. The new training experiments still lack detailed optimization and hardware settings.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including SpatialViz-Bench, ViewSpatial-Bench, DrivingVQA's associated work, DexVLG, and DreamVLA, while removing several background references, including Segment Anything and MMMU. Related-work discussion is shortened, but the positioning around comprehensive, psychology-grounded spatial evaluation remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and compresses existing introduction, taxonomy, dataset-construction, method, and evaluation prose. Method subsection titles change, Section 4.4 and Sections C.2–C.3 extend the narrative structure, and citation and heading styles change throughout. Appendix task definitions and prompt wording are retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds four substantive tables covering training, transfer, full-benchmark results, and human reliability. Existing tables are reformatted with captions above them, Table 4 moves, Figure 1's summary panel changes, and Table 1 drops the contextual BLINK-Spatial row. The document is extensively retypeset; appendix examples retain their content with altered rendering.

improvement.justification: Training comparisons and VSI-Bench transfer results provide useful validation absent from v1, while agreement statistics and human confidence intervals strengthen reliability reporting. However, missing training settings limit reproducibility, Florence-2 in the method text conflicts with SAM in Figure 5, and Table 9's 92.6% human accuracy conflicts with approximately 89% in its accompanying prose. These issues limit the overall quality gain.
